title: Eastern Air Lines 537
summary: On November 1, 1949, Eastern Air Lines Flight 537, a Douglas DC-4 on approach to Washington National Airport, collided in mid-air at 300 ft with a Lockheed P-38 Lightning being test-flown for the Bolivian Air Force, killing all 55 aboard the DC-4. The Civil Aeronautics Board found the P-38 pilot landed without proper clearance and failed to watch for conflicting traffic, while tower controllers also failed to warn Flight 537 of the developing traffic conflict in time.
probable_cause: The CAB found the primary causes were the P-38 pilot's decision to land without proper clearance and his failure to exercise normal vigilance for conflicting traffic; it also found tower controllers failed to notify Flight 537 earlier of the developing traffic situation, though this may not have changed the outcome.

factors.evidence: the P-38 pilot's decision to land without proper clearance
his failure to exercise normal vigilance in looking out for conflicting traffic

events.text: The P-38 requested permission to land due to engine trouble and was cleared by the controller to join the left traffic pattern, but instead flew south and entered a long straight-in approach.
The controller called Flight 537 ordering it to turn left onto a shorter final at the same time the P-38 entered its straight-in approach.
The P-38, considerably faster than the DC-4 on final, overtook Flight 537 a half mile southwest of the Runway 3 threshold.
The DC-4 was cut in half by the left propeller of the P-38 just forward of the trailing edge of the wing, killing all 55 aboard.

title: Linea Aeropostal Venezolana 253 (June 1956)

location.name: Atlantic Ocean off Asbury Park, New Jersey

summary: Flight 253 turned back to New York after Captain Plata reported the No. 2 propeller overspeeding and could not be feathered. While descending and dumping fuel off Asbury Park, escort crews saw the streaming fuel ignite near the No. 3 engine; the Super Constellation swerved, nosed over and plunged into the Atlantic, killing all 74 aboard. The board believed propeller vibration had damaged the wing near the fuel dump chute, providing the likely ignition source, but could not confirm it with certainty.
probable_cause: The board considered it most probable that vibration from the runaway No. 2 propeller damaged the wing structure near the fuel dump chute, providing the ignition source for the dumped fuel, though it could not determine this with certainty.

factors.evidence: Captain Plata reported the No. 2 propeller overspeeding and the crew declared an emergency, unable to feather it.

The airliner swerved violently to the right, nosed over, and plunged into the sea, exploding on impact

events.text: Captain Plata reported the No. 2 propeller, inboard on the port wing, was overspeeding, and radioed his intent to return to Idlewild.
The crew declared an emergency, stating they had been unable to feather the No. 2 propeller.
Captain Plata requested and received permission to dump fuel, and began doing so at 1:29.
The crews of both escort aircraft observed the streaming fuel catch fire near the No. 3 engine and erupt in a large fireball.
The airliner swerved violently to the right, nosed over, and plunged into the sea, exploding on impact 32 miles east of Asbury Park.

notes: Board could not confirm the ignition source with certainty; investigating agency not named.

title: 1956 Grand Canyon mid-air collision
summary: A TWA Constellation and United DC-7 collided over the Grand Canyon at 10:32 am in uncontrolled airspace. The two aircraft collided at an angle of about 25 degrees, and the DC-7's left wing clipped the Constellation's vertical stabilizer and fuselage, causing the tail assembly to break away. The Constellation entered a near-vertical terminal velocity dive and disintegrated on impact, while the DC-7 entered a rapidly descending left spiral and crashed into a cliff. All 128 people aboard both aircraft were killed.
probable_cause: The collision took place in uncontrolled airspace where it was the pilots' responsibility to maintain separation by 'see and be seen'. Investigation could not determine conclusively how much opportunity was available for the pilots to see and avoid each other due to uncertainty regarding high altitude visibility.

title: KLM 607-E
summary: KLM Flight 607-E, a Lockheed Super Constellation named Hugo de Groot on the second leg of a transatlantic trip from Amsterdam to New York, crashed into the Atlantic Ocean after departing Shannon Airport, Ireland, on 14 August 1958. Radio contact was lost about 35 minutes after takeoff, and a rescue operation later found light debris and recovered the remains of 34 of the 99 people aboard roughly 180 km northwest of Shannon. Irish and Dutch investigators could not pinpoint a definitive cause but believed the most likely explanation was an over-speeding outboard propeller, caused by metal particles obstructing an oil feed line regulator valve, which may have provoked a flight disturbance and caused the propeller to shear off.
probable_cause: Investigators could not determine a definitive cause but considered the most likely explanation to be a malfunctioning over-speeding outboard propeller, caused by metal particles obstructing oil feed line regulator valves, which may have provoked a flight disturbance and caused the propeller to shear off.

notes: Cause never conclusively determined; investigators only reached a probable hypothesis after considering bomb, electrical failure and pilot error.

title: American Airlines 320
summary: American Airlines Flight 320, a Lockheed L-188 Electra flying from Chicago to New York, crashed into the East River about 4,900 ft short of runway 22 while approaching LaGuardia Airport through a 400 ft overcast ceiling and fog, killing 65 of 73 aboard. The Civil Aeronautics Board found the crew, new to the Electra, flew below the intended approach path while the altimeter appeared to show a safe altitude; the Air Line Pilots Association instead blamed faulty instruments. It was the first crash involving the Electra type.
probable_cause: The Civil Aeronautics Board concluded the crew made mistakes that caused the crash, with the crew's inexperience on the Electra and poor weather conditions cited as contributing factors.

events.text: The LaGuardia approach controller advised the pilots of an overcast ceiling of 400 ft and visibility of 1.25 mi, and instructed them to prepare for approach to runway 22 over the East River.

LaGuardia tower gave the flight its final landing clearance for runway 22 when it was 2.8 mi from the airport; the crew acknowledged only with '320' and there were no further radio communications.
A witness in a car near the Whitestone Bridge saw the aircraft pass overhead only about 100 ft above the ground, lower than planes usually flew in the area.
Flying at 140 knots, the aircraft struck the East River about 4900 ft short of the runway.

title: Northwest Orient Airlines 710
summary: Northwest Airlines Flight 710, a Lockheed L-188 Electra flying from Chicago to Miami, broke up in midair over southern Indiana on March 17, 1960, after unexpectedly encountering clear-air turbulence at 18,000 ft; the right wing and part of the left wing separated and the aircraft plunged into farmland near Cannelton at over 600 mph, killing all 63 aboard. Investigators found the breakup closely resembled the 1959 Braniff Electra crash near Buffalo, Texas, and traced the cause to 'whirl mode' wing flutter: when an Electra's outboard engine mounting structure was damaged, high speed or turbulence could destroy the wing. The FAA restricted Electra operations and ordered Lockheed to redesign the structure.
probable_cause: The investigation attributed the in-flight breakup to whirl mode wing flutter: damage to an outboard engine's mounting structure, combined with high speed or turbulence, produced a destructive flutter that failed the wing -- the same unresolved defect implicated in the earlier Braniff Electra crash.

factors.evidence: The in-flight breakup of the Electra closely resembled the September 1959 crash of Braniff International Airways Flight 542 ... Investigators were unable to determine the cause at the time

the aircraft's right wing and part of the left wing separated, causing the fuselage to plummet and impact the ground

events.text: Flight 710 took off from Chicago Midway Airport at 2:38 p.m. with 57 passengers and a crew of 6.
At 3:13 p.m., passing the Scotland, Indiana waypoint at 18,000 ft, the crew reported to Indianapolis ARTC that the flight was proceeding normally.
Around the same time, U.S. Air Force B-57s operating nearby reported moderate to severe clear-air turbulence at high altitude, with one descending from 20,000-25,000 ft to 15,000 ft to escape it.

At about 3:20 p.m., in level flight at 400 mph, the aircraft's right wing separated from the fuselage, followed over six to ten seconds by the rest of the right wing and its engines; the outer left wing and its engine also broke away.

With its wings gone, the aircraft's momentum carried it more than 3 mi before it arced toward the ground, with an engine on the remaining left wing continuing to run at full power and accelerating the dive.
The aircraft struck farmland about 8 mi east of Cannelton, Indiana, nose-first at over 600 mph, leaving a crater about 15 ft deep and 30 ft wide.

title: 1960 New York air disaster
summary: On December 16, 1960, United Air Lines Flight 826, a Douglas DC-8 heading for Idlewild Airport, collided in midair with Trans World Airlines Flight 266, a Lockheed L-1049 Super Constellation descending toward LaGuardia Airport. The Constellation crashed on Miller Field in Staten Island and the DC-8 in Park Slope, Brooklyn, killing all 128 aboard the two aircraft and six people on the ground. The accident was the world's deadliest aviation disaster at the time and remains the deadliest accident in United Airlines history.
probable_cause: United 826 had only one operational VOR receiver after the other became inoperative, which presented difficulty for the pilots to identify the PRESTON intersection. ATC was not informed of the inoperative receiver. The aircraft was estimated to be traveling at 301 knots when it collided, several miles beyond the PRESTON clearance limit.

title: Sabena 548
summary: Sabena Flight 548, a Boeing 707 flying from New York to Brussels, made two aborted landing attempts at Brussels Airport on 15 February 1961 after a small aircraft had not yet cleared the runway. On a third circuit the aircraft's bank angle gradually increased until it reached a near-vertical bank at 1,500 ft; it then leveled its wings, pitched up abruptly, lost speed and spiraled nose-down into the ground near Berg, killing all 72 aboard and one person on the ground. Investigators could not conclusively determine the cause but believed the most likely explanation was a mechanical failure of the tail stabilizer-adjusting mechanism, possibly involving the wing spoilers.
probable_cause: The exact cause was never fully determined. Authorities agreed the most likely explanation was a mechanical failure of a flight-control mechanism, probably a malfunction of the wing spoilers or, as the FAA believed, the tail stabilizer-adjusting mechanism.

events.text: Near the runway threshold at a height of 900 ft, power was increased and the landing gear retracted after the approach was aborted because a small plane had not yet cleared the runway.
The 707 circled the airport and attempted to land on the adjoining Runway 25, which was not operational, but this second approach was also aborted.

The plane plunged into the ground less than two miles from the airport at 10:05 CET, and eyewitnesses said it exploded and burst into flames.

notes: Cause was never conclusively established; text presents FAA's stabilizer-failure hypothesis as the leading theory among several considered.

title: American Airlines 1
summary: American Airlines Flight 1 rolled over and crashed into Jamaica Bay two minutes after taking off from Idlewild Airport on 1 March 1962, killing all 87 passengers and eight crew aboard. During a left turn to 290 degrees at 1,600 ft, the Boeing 707 banked too sharply, rolled past 90 degrees, and entered a nearly vertical, upside-down dive before striking Pumpkin Patch Channel. The CAB traced the cause to a short circuit in wires damaged during manufacturing at a Bendix plant, producing a rudder malfunction that led to a loss of control from which the crew could not recover.
probable_cause: Rudder control system malfunction producing yaw, sideslip, and roll leading to a loss of control from which recovery was not effective; a rudder servo malfunction due to shorted wires was cited as the most likely abnormality.

events.text: The aircraft received instructions to taxi to Runway 31L at 09:54 EST.

In the course of the turn, at 1,600 ft, the aircraft banked too sharply, rolled past 90 degrees, and began an upside-down, nose-first descent in a nearly vertical dive.
The Boeing 707 crashed into Pumpkin Patch Channel, Jamaica Bay, at 10:08:49 while angled at 78 degrees, exploding on impact.

title: Flying Tiger Line 739
summary: Flying Tiger Line Flight 739, a Lockheed Super Constellation chartered by the US Army, disappeared on 16 March 1962 while en route from Guam to the Philippines with 107 military personnel and crew aboard. A civilian tanker observed what appeared to be an in-flight explosion. The Civil Aeronautics Board determined Flight 739 probably exploded in-flight based on tanker observations.

title: Air France 007
summary: Air France Flight 007, a Boeing 707 taking off from Orly on 3 June 1962, lifted off but the main landing gear remained on the ground. The crew attempted to abort the takeoff, using wheel brakes and reverse thrust to stop the aircraft. The aircraft skidded off the runway and struck the town of Villeneuve-le-Roi. Investigation indicated the elevator trim motor may have failed.

title: Alitalia 771
summary: Alitalia Flight 771, a multi-leg service from Sydney to Rome, crashed into a hill about 84 km north-east of Bombay on approach on 7-8 July 1962, killing all 94 aboard. Investigators found navigational errors led the captain, on his first familiarization trip over the Bangkok-Bombay leg, to believe he was closer to his destination than he actually was, causing a premature descent for a straight-in instrument approach at night; the aircraft continued down to 3,600 ft, below both the 9,000 ft minimum safety altitude and the 4,000 ft minimum initial approach altitude, before striking terrain.
probable_cause: Errors in navigation led the pilot to think he was closer to the point of descent than in reality, resulting in a premature descent for a straight-in instrument approach at night and controlled flight into terrain.

The aircraft crashed into a hill about 84 km north-east of Bombay while on approach, killing all 94 aboard.

summary: Varig Flight 810 crashed into the Laz Cruz Peak while maneuvering for an approach to Lima on 27 November 1962, killing all 97 aboard. An overestimate of seven minutes in the flight-planned time between Pisco and Lima left the Boeing 707 too high for a straight-in approach to runway 33, so ATC had the crew fly a 360-degree orbit and turns to intercept the ILS back course; during this extended maneuvering the aircraft deviated eight miles east of the published approach track and struck the peak at a heading of 333 degrees. Investigators suggested the pilot may have mistuned the Limatambo NDB for the Lima NDB.
probable_cause: A deviation, for reasons unknown, from the track prescribed for the instrument approach along the ILS back course of Lima-Callao Airport.

events.text: At 03:43 UTC the flight departed Rio en route to Lima carrying 80 passengers and 17 crew members.

At 08:30, with the flight at 12,000 ft directly overhead Las Palmas and still too high for a straight-in approach to runway 33, ATC had the crew fly a 360-degree orbit over Las Palmas.
The flight continued turning to intercept the ILS back course at a heading of 327 degrees before initiating a turn north.

No investigating agency named in the text.

title: Air India 101
summary: Air India Flight 101, a Boeing 707 named Kanchenjunga, crashed into Mont Blanc in France on 24 January 1966 while on approach to Geneva. The pilot, thinking he had passed Mont Blanc, started to descend and flew into the Mont Blanc massif at 4750 meters elevation. All 117 people aboard were killed.
probable_cause: The pilot believed the aircraft had passed Mont Blanc when instructed to descend for Geneva, but the aircraft had not yet cleared the mountain. The crew had one VOR receiver unserviceable and failed to confirm their position before descending.

The pilot, thinking that he had passed Mont Blanc, started to descend.
The aircraft descended toward the Mont Blanc massif.
The Boeing 707 operating the flight accidentally crashed into Mont Blanc in France.

title: Canadian Pacific Air Lines 402
summary: Flight 402, a DC-8-43 flying Hong Kong-Tokyo-Vancouver, held near Haneda for 38 minutes and cancelled one approach as visibility fluctuated below minima at night. After diverting toward Taipei and being told visibility had improved to a 3,000 ft runway visual range, the captain flew a second approach; advised the aircraft was 20 ft low near the runway, it continued below and parallel to the glide slope before a sharp descent struck eleven approach lights and the seawall short of the threshold. The pilot lost control after impact and 64 of 72 aboard were killed. Investigators found no tower fault, attributing the crash to pilot error and possible optical illusion from poor visibility.
probable_cause: "Pilot misjudged landing approach under unusually difficult weather conditions," with poor visibility cited as a possible source of an optical illusion; the investigation found no fault with the airport control tower.

events.text: At 19:58, after holding 38 minutes and cancelling one approach when visibility dropped, the pilot asked ATC to divert to Songshan Airport, Taiwan.
At 20:05, climbing through 11,500 ft toward Taipei, the pilot was told visibility at Haneda had improved to a runway visual range of 3,000 ft, and decided on another approach.

Advised it was 20 ft low near the runway, the aircraft nevertheless continued 20 ft below and parallel to the glide slope, and after passing the precision minimum the crew requested reduced runway light intensity.
The aircraft made a sharp descent and, 2,800 ft from the runway threshold, its landing gear struck eleven approach lights before hitting the seawall, and the pilot lost control.

title: BOAC 911
summary: BOAC Flight 911, a Boeing 707 departing Tokyo Haneda for Hong Kong, encountered severe clear-air turbulence over Mount Fuji and disintegrated in mid-air on 5 March 1966. The structural failure began with the vertical stabilizer attachment failing under extreme aerodynamic loads. All 124 occupants were killed.
probable_cause: The aircraft encountered abnormally severe clear-air turbulence over Gotemba City which imposed gust loads considerably in excess of the aircraft's structural design, causing the vertical stabilizer to fail and leading to airframe breakup in flight.

factors.evidence: the vertical stabiliser attachment to the fuselage failed first

stress cracking was found in the vertical stabiliser bolt holes
Subsequent inspections on Boeing 707 and similar Boeing 720 aircraft revealed this was a common problem

events.text: The aircraft began taxiing at 13:50 and took off into the northwest wind at 13:58.
After takeoff, the aircraft made a continuous climbing right turn over Tokyo Bay and rolled out on a southwest heading.
At an altitude of approximately 16000 ft, well above the 12388 ft mountain peak, the aircraft encountered strong turbulence.
The vertical stabiliser attachment to the fuselage failed first, and the ventral fin and all four engine pylons failed due to leftward over-stress.
The aircraft entered a flat spin, with the forward fuselage section and the outer starboard wing breaking off shortly before impact.
Flight 911 left a debris field 16 km long after impact with the ground.

title: Stockport air disaster
summary: British Midland Flight 542, a Canadair C-4 Argonaut returning holidaymakers from Palma de Mallorca to Manchester, lost its No. 3 and 4 engines over Stockport during a second approach after an earlier overshoot; the No. 4 propeller feathered but the No. 3 kept windmilling, and the aircraft became uncontrollable and crashed at Hopes Carr, killing 72 of 84 aboard. Ruptured fuel tanks fed a fire through the cabin. The AIB found the double engine failure was caused by fuel starvation from an unrecognised flaw in the Argonaut's cross-feed fuel system, with poorly placed cockpit selectors; crew fatigue after a nearly 13-hour duty day was a third contributory factor.
probable_cause: The AIB found the double engine failure resulted from fuel starvation caused by an unrecognised flaw in the Argonaut's fuel cross-feed system, whose poorly placed, unclear cockpit selectors could cause inadvertent cross-feed and exhaust a pair of tanks; crew fatigue was a contributory factor.

events.text: The Argonaut left Palma de Mallorca at 5:00 am carrying holidaymakers back to Manchester Airport.

The aircraft became uncontrollable and crashed at 10:09 am local time in a small open area at Hopes Carr, close to the town centre.
A fire started towards the rear of the aircraft after the fuel tanks had ruptured and worked back through the cabin, killing most of the fuel-soaked passengers.

title: Aeroflot 2230
summary: Aeroflot Flight 2230, an Ilyushin Il-18V flying from Sverdlovsk to Tashkent, suffered an engine fire shortly after takeoff on 16 November 1967, and the propeller could not be feathered. Maneuverability at maximum takeoff weight was degraded by the drag of the windmilling propeller, and the crew lost control at a height of 200 m while climbing. The aircraft crashed into a plowed field in a 37-degree right bank at 440 km/h, killing all 107 aboard; the wreckage's complete disintegration complicated the investigation.

title: 1968 Indian Air Force An-12 crash
summary: Indian Air Force An-12 Flight 203, flown by Flight Lieutenant Harkewal Singh and Squadron Leader Pran Nath Malhotra, was on approach to Leh from Chandigarh when the pilot turned back due to inclement weather; the aircraft went missing with its last radio contact over the Rohtang Pass and was declared lost after searches failed to find the wreck. Expeditions between 2003 and 2024 have recovered remains and wreckage from Himalayan glaciers, confirming the aircraft went down in terrain at about 18,000 ft.

the aircraft then went missing with the last radio contact over the Rohtang Pass

events.text: Flight 203 was on approach to Leh when the pilot decided to turn back due to inclement weather.
The aircraft went missing, with the last radio contact over the Rohtang Pass, and was declared missing after the failure to find the wreck.
On 18 August 2019, a joint Indian Army and Air Force team recovered aircraft parts including the aero engine, fuselage, propeller and a cockpit door.

notes: No formal investigation finding stated; aircraft was missing for decades, only wreckage/remains recovered.

title: South African Airways 228
summary: South African Airways Flight 228, a new Boeing 707 taking off from Windhoek on 20 April 1968 in a dark, moonless night with no ground lights, initially climbed to 650 ft then leveled off and started to descend. Fifty seconds after takeoff the aircraft flew into terrain at approximately 271 knots. The crew failed to maintain safe airspeed and altitude by not observing flight instruments.
probable_cause: The captain and first officer failed to maintain a safe airspeed and altitude and a positive climb by not observing flight instruments during takeoff. Loss of situational awareness in dark, moonless night conditions contributed; the crew misread altitude and vertical speed indicators.

events.text: The aircraft took off from Windhoek on runway 08 at 18:49 GMT into a dark, moonless night.
The aircraft initially climbed to an altitude of 650 ft above ground level, then leveled off.
The aircraft began to descend while the crew had no visual reference in the dark conditions.
Fifty seconds after take-off, the aircraft flew into the ground in flight configuration at approximately 271 knots.
The aircraft's four engines were the first parts to touch the ground, creating four deep gouges in the soil.
Two fires erupted immediately when the aircraft's fuel tanks ignited.

title: 1968 Kham Duc C-130 shootdown
summary: A USAF C-130B commanded by Major Bernard L. Bucher was shot down on 12 May 1968 while evacuating civilians from the besieged Kham Duc camp. After landing under fire and loading 150 evacuees, Bucher took off northward, unaware North Vietnamese forces were concentrated there; under fire from 12.7mm and 14.5mm heavy machine guns the aircraft shook violently out of control and crashed into a ravine less than a mile from the airstrip, killing everyone aboard.

Major Bucher took off in a northward direction, unaware that North Vietnamese forces were concentrated in that area.

Under intense anti-aircraft fire from 12.7mm and 14.5mm heavy machine guns, the aircraft shook violently out of control and crashed into a ravine less than a mile from the airstrip, killing everyone aboard.

title: Air France 1611
summary: Air France Flight 1611, a Sud Aviation Caravelle, took off from Ajaccio at 10:09 on 11 September 1968, bound for Nice. The flight was initially without incident and weather conditions were sunny. At 10:30 local time, on descending between flight level 90 to flight level 70, the flight crew declared an emergency mentioning a fire on board. The radio and radar contact was lost after a final contact at 10:33, and a kerosene slick and floating debris were discovered, confirming that the plane had crashed into the sea with all 95 people aboard.
probable_cause: The report surmised that the loss of the aircraft was caused by a fire in the passenger toilet caused either by a defective water heater or a cigarette discarded in a waste bin. The direct cause of loss of control could not be definitively established: it may be related to the pilots' physical incapacity caused either by toxic gas emissions or by passengers invading the cockpit.

A kerosene slick and floating debris were discovered in the Mediterranean Sea, confirming that the plane had crashed into the sea.

title: Viasa 742
summary: Viasa Flight 742, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9-32 registered YV-C-AVD, was on the Maracaibo-to-Miami leg of a flight from Caracas when it began its takeoff roll at 12:00 on 16 March 1969. Heading toward the Ziruma district, the aircraft failed to gain altitude and its left engine struck a power pole; as the plane banked left a reflector struck the fuel tank, spilling fuel, and after hitting a second power pole the left wing was ripped off and the left engine exploded into flames before the plane crashed in La Trinidad, Maracaibo. All 84 people aboard and 71 more on the ground were killed. Investigators attributed the crash to faulty sensors along with runway and takeoff calculations made from erroneous information, which left the aircraft overloaded by more than 5,000 pounds for the prevailing conditions.
probable_cause: The cause of the crash was attributed to faulty sensors, along with runway and take-off calculations made from erroneous information, which resulted in the aircraft being overloaded by more than 5,000 pounds for the prevailing conditions.

events.text: The aircraft arrived at Maracaibo at 10:30; Captain Maldonado became pilot in command of the last leg and the aircraft was loaded with 12000 kg of jet fuel.
Flight 742 began its takeoff roll at 12:00, overloaded because of erroneous runway and take-off calculations.
As the DC-9 headed toward the Ziruma district it failed to gain altitude, and the plane's left engine struck a power pole.
As the plane banked left a reflector struck the fuel tank, spilling fuel; after hitting another power pole the left wing was ripped off and the left engine exploded into flames.

notes: 71 additional fatalities occurred on the ground; occupants/fatalities here reflect only those aboard the aircraft.

title: 1969 Aswan Ilyushin Il-18 crash
summary: An Ilyushin Il-18 operated by United Arab Airlines, carrying Hajj pilgrims from Jeddah to Aswan, made two unsuccessful landing attempts in darkness with visibility reduced to 2-3 kilometers by a sandstorm on 20 March 1969. On a third approach the aircraft banked right and hit the left side of the runway, tearing off the starboard wing; the resulting fuel spillage caused the wreckage to burst into flames, killing 100 of the 105 aboard. Investigators found the pilot had descended below the minimum safe altitude without the runway lights clearly in sight, and cited fatigue from continuous working hours without suitable rest as a contributory factor.

title: Mexicana de Aviación 704

summary: Flight 704, a Boeing 727 flying from Mexico City to Monterrey, was descending toward Del Norte airport in cloudy weather with a 500-foot ceiling and haze when the crew asked whether the Ciénega de Flores beacon was operating and were told it was off from a power outage, yet reported receiving a signal resembling it. After reporting the airport in sight, the crew began final approach and struck the Cerro del Fraile mountain range, killing all 79; the last CVR minutes were missing, so investigators could not determine the cause of the deviation.

The crew asked if the radio beacon at Ciénega de Flores was operating, and were told it was not functioning due to an electrical power outage.
Flight 704 then reported that, for some reason, they received a signal similar to the signal from this beacon.
The aircraft ended up destroyed in the Cerro del Fraile mountain range, killing all 79 people on board.

notes: Investigating board could not determine cause of deviation; last CVR minutes were missing.

title: 1969 Yukhnov mid-air collision
summary: On 23 June 1969, an Ilyushin Il-14M operating as Aeroflot Flight 831 collided in mid-air with an Antonov An-12BP of the Soviet Air Force over Yukhnovsky District. The Il-14 disobeyed ATC instructions and climbed to 3000 m to avoid turbulence, where the An-12 formation was flying. All 120 occupants of both aircraft perished.
probable_cause: The pilots of the Il-14 disobeyed instructions from air traffic control and climbed to the altitude of 3000 m to avoid turbulence and clouds, where the formation of An-12s were flying. The An-12 pilots also flew slightly lower than their assigned altitude of 3000 m, contributing to the collision.

events.text: At 13:25 the An-12 involved in the accident took off from Kedainiai Air Base as the last one in a formation of four.
At 14:07 the Ilyushin Il-14 took off from Bykovo Airport and climbed to the assigned altitude of 2700 m.
At 14:40:55 the crew of Il-14 contacted air traffic control and requested permission to climb to 3300 m due to severe turbulence and cumulus clouds.
Due to the An-12s at 3000 m, the controller instead offered permission to descend to 2700 m, but the pilots of the Il-14 declined.
At 14:52 the two aircraft collided over Yukhnov, first striking at the wingtips, then the An-12's nose colliding with the right horizontal stabilizer of the Il-14.
The An-12 lost the right wing and right wing engines from the impact, causing it to spin to the ground, while the Il-14 lost part of the right wing and the upper part of the fuselage.

title: Air France 212 (1969)
summary: Air France Flight 212, a Boeing 707 on the Caracas-to-Pointe-à-Pitre leg of a Santiago-to-Paris routing, took off from Caracas at 19:02 local time and about one minute later, at roughly 3,000 feet, plunged into the sea and sank in 160 feet of water, killing all 62 aboard. The BEA never published a report and the documents remain classified until 2029, so the cause was never established; theories include an evasive maneuver around a nearby Avro 748 followed by loss of control, a bomb, spatial disorientation, in-flight fire, engine failure and fuel contamination.

Theories about the crash have included a maneuver to avoid colliding with a nearby Avro 748 followed by loss of control, and a bomb-related explosion.

notes: BEA never published its report; cause unconfirmed among competing theories cited in the article.

title: Olympic Airways 954
summary: Olympic Airways Flight 954, a Douglas DC-6B on a domestic flight from Chania, Crete, to Athens, struck Mount Paneio near Keratea at approximately 2,000 feet with its undercarriage retracted while on approach to Athens on 8 December 1969. Rain and high winds prevailed at the time, and all 85 passengers and 5 crew aboard were killed. Investigators ruled that the flight crew had deviated from the proper track and descended below the minimum safe altitude while making an ILS approach.

title: Aeroflot U-45

location.name: mountainside 32 km northeast of Samarkand Airport

summary: Aeroflot Flight U-45, an Il-18 flying Tashkent-Samarkand in instrument meteorological conditions, was cleared to descend by approach control, but the controller misread the radar and reported the aircraft 31 km out when it was actually 42-44 km, prompting a premature descent before the mountain range was crossed. The crew, whose own radar was degraded by weather, missed a clue that the reported distances implied an impossible speed; at 14:42 the Il-18 struck a mountainside at 380 km/h, killing 92 of 106 aboard. The controller's misreading of the display scale was the primary cause, compounded by subpar ATC training.

title: Dominicana DC-9 air disaster
summary: Dominicana de Aviación Flight 603 crashed into the Caribbean Sea shortly after taking off from Santo Domingo for San Juan on 15 February 1970, killing all 97 passengers and five crew aboard. Two minutes after departure the right engine flamed out; while the crew were preparing to turn back, the left engine also flamed out, and the DC-9 descended into the sea about two miles south of the airport. The investigation concluded the sequential failure of both engines was caused by fuel contamination due to water ingress.

title: Dan-Air 1903

location.name: Les Agudes, Serralada del Montseny, near Arbúcies

summary: Dan-Air Flight 1903 crashed into the Serralada del Montseny near Arbúcies during a descent toward Barcelona on 3 July 1970, killing all 112 aboard the Comet 4. The crew mistakenly reported passing the Sabadell NDB while still 28 nmi north of it over mountainous terrain; the controller, misled by a radar echo from another aircraft over Sabadell, did not notice the error and cleared the crew to keep descending to 2800 ft. The aircraft struck beech trees on the Les Agudes peak at about 3800 ft.
probable_cause: An involuntary mutual error between crew and ATC: erroneous position reporting by the crew combined with a radar echo from another aircraft near Sabadell led the controller to believe the Comet had passed the beacon, and this could not be corrected before the aircraft struck high terrain.

events.text: Flight 1903 departed Manchester Airport at 16:08 BST and encountered air traffic control delays in the Paris area, resulting in a change of route.
Radio contact was established with Barcelona Area Control Centre at 17:53 local time, and the crew was cleared to descend from Flight Level 220 to FL090.
Six minutes later the flight was handed to Barcelona approach control, which cleared the crew to overfly the Sabadell NDB and descend further to FL060.
While carrying out the turn, the crew reported in error that they had passed the Sabadell NDB, though they were still 28 nautical miles north of it, over the Serralada del Montseny.
Barcelona ATC mistook the radar echo of another aircraft overflying Sabadell for the Dan-Air Comet and cleared the crew to continue descending to 2800 ft.
At about 19:05 CEST the Comet struck a group of beech trees on the northeast slopes of the Les Agudes peak at an altitude of about 3800 ft and was destroyed in the explosion.

notes: Agency AAIB inferred from the UK AAIB report link; not explicitly named in the article text.

title: Air Canada 621
summary: Air Canada Flight 621, a Douglas DC-8 landing at Toronto on 5 July 1970, touched down hard which ruptured the right fuel tanks. The investigation attributed the accident to pilot error and non-compliance with spoiler deployment procedures, where the first officer deployed spoilers during the flare instead of arming them.

title: Aviogenex 130
summary: Aviogenex Flight 130, an international charter from Gatwick to Rijeka, took off at 16:33 GMT and suffered structural failure during landing on 23 May 1971. The Tupolev Tu-134A flipped over and caught fire. Investigation found that the crew might have suffered an optical illusion due to heavy showers and dusk that could have led them to believe the runway was closer and lower than it actually was. The crew executed an overly steep and fast descent in the last phase of final approach, causing a hard touchdown and breakage of the right wing, killing 78 out of 83 people.
probable_cause: Optical illusion caused by dusk, rain and water on runway led the crew to believe they were closer and higher from the runway than actually the case. The crew made a sharp nose-down input and reduced power to idle in the final phase, causing the aircraft to reach excessive speed and contact the runway with forces that broke the right wing.

title: British European Airways 548
summary: Hawker Siddeley Trident entered a deep stall during initial climb shortly after takeoff from Heathrow and descended steeply until crashing near Staines. summary: Japan Air Lines Flight 123, a Boeing 747, suffered explosive decompression 12 minutes after takeoff from Tokyo when an aft pressure bulkhead repaired seven years earlier finally failed, rupturing all four hydraulic systems and ejecting the vertical stabiliser. summary: During approach to Cali, the crew opted for a straight-in approach and mistakenly cleared all programmed approach waypoints from the FMS. The pilots selected the wrong radiobeacon identifier (R instead of ROZO), causing the autopilot to fly toward Bogotá. The aircraft descended into a valley north of Cali with ground proximity warning activated 12 seconds before impact. The crew attempted to climb clear, but fully extended speed brakes prevented adequate rate of climb, leading to stick shaker activation and terrain impact at 8,920 feet.
probable_cause: Navigational errors by the flight crew, specifically the selection of the wrong radiobeacon identifier and the failure to retract speed brakes during the escape maneuver.

factors.evidence: pilots mistakenly cleared all the programmed approach waypoints from the flight plan in the aircraft FMS
By selecting "R" from the waypoint list, the captain caused the autopilot to start flying a course to Bogotá
By the time the error was detected, the aircraft was in a valley running roughly north–south
pilots had already passed over Tulua VOR without detecting the navigation error
neither pilot had remembered to disengage the previously deployed speed brakes, which were fully extended
stick shaker mechanically vibrates the control yoke to warn the flight crew of an imminent aerodynamic stall
aircraft struck trees at about 8920 ft above mean sea level on the east side of the 9000 ft mountain

events.text: Flight 965 took off at 6:35 pm EST nearly two hours late due to winter storm delay and seasonal congestion
Pilots agreed to straight-in approach to runway 19 hoping to make up time, then mistakenly cleared all programmed approach waypoints from FMS flight plan
Pilots selected Tulua VOR identifier ULQ into FMS flight plan after already passing over it
Captain selected the "R" identifier from the waypoint list instead of ROZO
Ground proximity warning system activated announcing imminent terrain collision, sounding an alarm
First officer disengaged autopilot within one second of warning, captain attempted to climb clear of mountain
Take-off power selected, pitch increased to 20.6 degrees upwards, but previously deployed speed brakes remained fully extended
Aircraft struck trees at about 8920 ft with stick shaker activated, flying at 187 knots and pitch 28 degrees

title: 1996 Air Africa crash
summary: Moscow Airways Antonov An-32B overran the runway while attempting to take off fully fueled and overloaded from N'Dolo Airport's short runway. The aircraft failed to achieve sufficient speed to bring its nose up, began to lift, and crashed into the Simbazikita produce market. The full fuel load ignited, creating a massive post-impact fire. Ground fatalities were estimated between 225 and 348, making this the deadliest aviation accident in African history and deadliest by ground casualties outside of terrorist attacks.
probable_cause: The aircraft was overloaded and fully fueled while attempting to take off from N'Dolo Airport's short runway. The aircraft did not achieve sufficient speed to bring its nose up yet began to lift prematurely, resulting in loss of control and crash into the market below.

factors.evidence: Aircraft attempted to take off fully fuelled and overloaded from N'Dolo Airport's short runway.
An-32B did not achieve sufficient speed to bring nose up yet began to lift.
Aircraft overran the runway at N'Dolo Airport.
Full fuel load ignited in crash into market, creating massive fire.

events.text: Aircraft begins takeoff roll from N'Dolo Airport's short runway while fully fueled and overloaded.
Aircraft does not achieve sufficient speed to bring nose up yet begins to lift, losing control.
Aircraft crashes into Simbazikita produce market full of shacks, pedestrians and cars.

notes: Limited investigation report available; ground fatality count unclear
Flight number not documented in source
Limited technical details on aircraft configuration

title: Birgenair 301

agencies.name: Dominican Republic General Directorate of Civil Aviation

summary: Birgenair Flight 301, a Boeing 757 chartered from Puerto Plata to Frankfurt, crashed into the Atlantic shortly after takeoff on 6 February 1996, killing all 189 aboard. Investigators concluded a pitot tube, likely blocked by a wasp nest after the aircraft sat idle for 20 days without its covers, fed the captain's airspeed indicator false and increasing readings while the first officer's showed the correct, decreasing speed. Confused by conflicting overspeed and stall warnings, the captain reduced thrust believing the plane was too fast, triggering the stick shaker and a stall from which the crew did not recover.
probable_cause: The probable cause was the flight crew's failure to recognize and react to a blocked captain's pitot tube, most likely obstructed by a wasp nest, which produced erroneous, increasing airspeed indications that led the crew to reduce thrust into an aerodynamic stall.

factors.evidence: One of the three pitot tubes used to measure airspeed was blocked, most likely by a mud dauber wasp nest built inside it.
The aircraft had sat unused for 20 days, and its pitot covers were removed two days before the accident for an engine test run.
The captain's airspeed indicator showed over 300 knots and increasing while the first officer's correctly showed 220 knots decreasing.
Confused by the contradictory readings, the captain reduced thrust believing the aircraft was flying too fast.
The reduced thrust immediately triggered the 757's stick shaker stall alert.
The pilots should have followed existing procedures and aborted the takeoff once their airspeed indicators showed significant disagreement.
As the plane neared a stall its path became unstable and it started descending.

events.text: During the takeoff roll at 23:42 the captain found his airspeed indicator malfunctioning but chose not to abort the takeoff.
The autopilot engaged one minute 30 seconds into the flight; about ten seconds later rudder ratio and Mach airspeed trim warnings appeared.
The captain's ASI showed over 300 knots and increasing while the first officer's showed 220 knots decreasing, and an overspeed warning sounded.
Climbing through 4,700 ft with his ASI reading 350 knots, the confused captain reduced thrust, believing the plane too fast.
The reduced thrust immediately triggered the stick shaker stall alert, and the autopilot disengaged as the aircraft neared a stall.
As the plane became unstable and began descending, the controller called the flight and the first officer only replied "Stand by."

title: Faucett 251
summary: Faucett Perú Flight 251 crashed on approach to Arequipa at night after the crew received an outdated barometric altimeter setting. The aircraft impacted terrain 2 kilometers short of the runway, with the crew unaware they were flying nearly 1000 feet lower than displayed.
probable_cause: Crew issued outdated barometric altimeter setting after bypassing ILS signal, causing altitude misjudgment and controlled flight into terrain during night approach in poor visibility.

factors.evidence: the crew had been issued an outdated barometric altimeter setting after bypassing an ILS signal
The flight crew asked for the lights of the runway to be brightened as they could not see them when they should
they had the wrong impression the aircraft was flying at 9500 ft, when it actually was at 8640 ft
The airplane crashed into hills at 8200 ft, approximately 2 km short of the runway

events.text: The aircraft was on a VOR/DME approach to Rodríguez Ballón International Airport's runway 09, at night, in rain and mist, with thunderstorms reported in the area.
The flight crew asked for the lights of the runway to be brightened as they could not see them when they should on normal approach.

It was found that the crew had been issued an outdated barometric altimeter setting after bypassing an ILS signal, causing them to fly almost 1000 ft lower than the altitude they believed they were flying at.
The airplane crashed into hills at 8200 ft, approximately 2 km short of the runway.

title: ValuJet 592
summary: ValuJet Flight 592 crashed into the Florida Everglades about ten minutes after departing Miami on May 11, 1996. A fire developed in the cargo compartment caused by 144 expired chemical oxygen generators placed in cargo compartment boxes marked COMAT by maintenance contractor SabreTech. The fire caused progressive failure of the DC-9's electrical and flight control systems. All 110 people on board were killed, making it the deadliest aviation accident in Florida history.
probable_cause: Just before takeoff, 144 expired chemical oxygen generators were placed in the cargo compartment by ValuJet's maintenance contractor SabreTech, which violated Federal Aviation Administration regulations. The fire in the cargo compartment caused progressive failure of electrical and flight control systems leading to loss of control and crash.

factors.evidence: A fire developed in the cargo compartment caused by mislabeled and improperly stored chemical oxygen generators.
A flight attendant informed the crew of a fire in the passenger cabin.
144 expired chemical oxygen generators were placed in the cargo compartment in five boxes marked COMAT by maintenance contractor SabreTech.
The flight data recorder indicated progressive failure of the DC-9's electrical and flight control systems.

events.text: At 2:04 p.m. EDT, the DC-9 departed from Runway 9L and began a normal climb
At 2:10 p.m., passengers began to smell smoke and pilots heard a loud bang in their headsets
The sag in electrical power was determined to be the result of an explosion of a tire in the cargo hold
Kubeck and Hazen immediately asked air traffic control to return to Miami
Flight 592 disappeared from radar and crashed into the Everglades at a speed in excess of 507 mph

title: TWA 800
summary: TWA Flight 800, a Boeing 747 flying from New York to Rome via Paris, exploded in flight and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off East Moriches, New York, twelve minutes after takeoff on 17 July 1996, killing all 230 aboard. The four-year NTSB investigation concluded that flammable vapors in the center fuel tank ignited, likely from a short circuit, after finding arcing in the fuel quantity indication system wiring that enters the tank; the captain had remarked on 'crazy' FQIS readings shortly before the explosion.
probable_cause: The NTSB determined the probable cause was an explosion of flammable fuel/air vapors in the center wing fuel tank, most likely ignited by a short circuit, with evidence of arcing found in the fuel quantity indication system wiring that enters the tank.

factors.evidence: Problems with the aircraft's wiring were found, including evidence of arcing in the fuel quantity indication system (FQIS) wiring that enters the tank.
The report's conclusion was that the probable cause of the accident was the explosion of flammable fuel vapors in the center fuel tank.
Several wide-ranging recommendations were made, which were incorporated into newer US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) standards.
The Boeing 747-100 performing this flight exploded and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean near East Moriches, New York, twelve minutes after takeoff.

events.text: About two minutes and thirty seconds before the explosion, the captain remarked about 'crazy' readings from the fuel quantity indication system.
At approximately 8:31 p.m. EDT, twelve minutes after takeoff, the Boeing 747 exploded and crashed into the Atlantic Ocean near East Moriches, New York.
NTSB investigators found evidence of arcing in the fuel quantity indication system wiring that enters the center fuel tank, a likely ignition source for the flammable vapors.
All 230 people on board were killed when the aircraft broke apart and crashed into the ocean, the deadliest air disaster investigation in U.S. history up to that time.
The four-year NTSB investigation approved its Aircraft Accident Report on August 23, 2000, and its recommendations were incorporated into new FAA fuel-tank safety standards.

title: Vnukovo Airlines 2801
summary: On approach to Svalbard Airport, the crew used outdated Jeppesen charts and set both HSIs to magnetic runway heading 283 degrees without using the localizer course. During the inbound turn, lateral deviation from the centerline grew due to inadequate wind drift correction. The aircraft reached Advent at 1,524 meters and turned late, resulting in a left (northeast) deviation from the correct track. Navigation at 1,524 m minimum altitude led to aircraft striking ground at Operafjellet during final approach, 3.7 km from the centerline.
probable_cause: A series of small navigational errors caused the aircraft to be 3.7 km from the approach centerline at the time of impact. The crew did not attempt to intercept the correct magnetic course and were probably not aware of VHF direction finding available at the airport.

factors.evidence: lateral deviation from the centerline at the time of impact was 3.7 km
crew did not attempt to intercept the magnetic course 155 degrees outbound from Advent
aircrew was probably not aware of VHF direction finding available at the airport and have not used it to confirm aircraft position
additional request for use of Runway 10 was again not understood because of the misunderstanding of the term runway in use
From 3000 m until impact, the flight was carried out in instrument meteorological conditions
aircraft reached 1524 m minimum altitude to Advent before striking ground at Operafjellet

events.text: Aircraft reached 1524 m minimum altitude to Advent, the initial approach altitude
Aircraft began base turn to magnetic heading 160 degrees but turn was started late resulting in aircraft flying northeast of correct outbound track
Crew started inbound turn but lateral deviation from correct track persisted
Aircraft descended to minimum altitude in instrument meteorological conditions from 3000 m
Aircraft struck ground at Operafjellet during final approach, 3.7 km from approach centerline

notes: Exact times from text provide clock values
Lateral deviation of 3.7 km is specific measurement from report

title: ADC Airlines 86
summary: ADC Airlines Flight 086 was descending to 16000 ft when Triax Flight 185 was assigned a conflicting altitude at 15000 ft. The Lagos ATC controller made a radar separation error, thinking Flight 086 was at 10000 ft when it was actually descending to 16000 ft. Flight 086's TCAS warned of traffic and the crew attempted evasive action. Following the TCAS alert, Captain Sama took control, but ATC directed a heading that led to loss of control and the aircraft crashed inverted in Lagos Lagoon at high speed.
probable_cause: Air traffic control separation error combined with loss of control during evasive maneuver.

factors.evidence: crew of the Boeing 727-231 operating the flight lost control of the aircraft while avoiding a mid-air collision on approach
controller immediately asked Flight 086 to redirect its heading to 300
pilot was also found to be at fault for proceeding on a heading of 330
TCAS of Flight 086 sounded an alert, warning the flight crews to reduce descent and start climbing in order to prevent a collision with Flight 185

events.text: Flight 086 took off from Port Harcourt and climbed to 24000 ft.
As the flight was approaching Lagos, ATC cleared Flight 086 to descend to 16000 ft.
The TCAS of Flight 086 sounded an alert, warning crews to reduce descent and start climbing.
Captain Sama immediately took over as the TCAS sounded the alert and the crew noticed the incoming Triax Flight 185.
ATC asked Flight 086 to maintain heading 300 while still descending toward an altitude conflict.
The aircraft lost control and crashed inverted at a very high speed into Lagos Lagoon.

title: Charkhi Dadri mid-air collision
summary: Saudia Flight 763, a Boeing 747 climbing out of Delhi, collided almost head-on over Charkhi Dadri on 12 November 1996 with Kazakhstan Airlines Flight 1907, an Ilyushin Il-76 descending toward Delhi, killing all 349 aboard both aircraft. The Lahoti Commission found the Kazakh crew, relying on a radio operator due to poor English skills, failed to level off at their assigned altitude and kept descending toward the Saudia jet, compounded by crew resource management failures; Delhi's radar had no altitude readout.
probable_cause: The Kazakh Il-76 crew's failure to maintain its cleared altitude, worsened by poor English comprehension of ATC instructions and crew resource management failures, caused the collision with the climbing Saudia 747.

factors.evidence: Contributing factors included three specific incidents of failures in crew resource management by the Kazakh crew.
Poor English language skills in the Kazakh cockpit resulted in inadequate interpretation of ATC directions.
The Kazakh crew reported reaching 15,000 feet, but the aircraft was actually higher, at 16,348 ft, and still descending.
Delhi airport lacked a secondary surveillance radar; the primary radar gave distance and bearing but not altitude.
The Il-76's left wing sliced through the 747's engines while the 747's stabilizer sliced off the Il-76's tail.

events.text: Saudia 763 departed Delhi at 18:32 and was cleared to an initial altitude of 10,000 ft.
Controller Dutta cleared the descending Kazakh Il-76 to 15,000 ft when 74 nmi from the beacon.
Dutta cleared the climbing Saudia 747, on the same airway opposite direction, to 14,000 ft.
The Kazakh crew reported reaching 15,000 ft, though it was actually still descending through 16,348 ft.
Dutta warned of Saudia traffic at ten miles; Radio Operator Repp only replied "Now looking 1907" without confirming altitude.
A USAF crew reported a big explosion; the Il-76's left wing sliced through the 747's engines as its stabilizer severed the Il-76's tail.

notes: Record represents the Saudia 747 side of the collision; Kazakh Il-76 details described in summary/factors only

title: Korean Air 801

route.to_name: Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport

summary: Korean Air Flight 801, a Boeing 747-300 flying from Seoul to Guam, crashed into Bijia Peak on approach to Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport on August 6, 1997, after Captain Park continued a non-precision approach in heavy rain despite the glideslope being out of service. First officer Song and flight engineer Nam noticed the steep descent and said the airport was not in sight, but the captain proceeded until the aircraft struck terrain below the minimum safe altitude, killing 229 of the 254 aboard.
probable_cause: The NTSB cited poor communication between the flight crew as the probable cause, along with the captain's poor decision-making on the non-precision approach.

factors.evidence: The glideslope Instrument Landing System (ILS) for runway 6L was out of service, but Captain Park mistakenly believed it was in service.
Captain Park managed to pick up a signal that was later identified to be from an irrelevant electronic device on the ground.
It was raining heavily in Guam, so visibility was considerably reduced, and the crew attempted an instrument landing.
Despite protests from Nam that the detected signal was not the glide-slope indicator, Park continued the approach.
The aircraft descended below the minimum safe altitude of 1440 ft during its landing approach.
The aircraft crashed into Bijia Peak just short of a VHF omnidirectional range navigation beacon about 3 nmi short of the runway, at an altitude of 660 ft.

events.text: At 1:35 am, Captain Park picked up a signal he believed was the runway 6L glideslope, though the ILS glideslope was actually out of service.
First officer Song and flight engineer Nam noticed the aircraft was descending very steeply and remarked several times that the airport was not in sight.
Flight engineer Nam protested that the detected signal was not the glide-slope indicator, but Captain Park continued the approach.
At 1:42 am the aircraft crashed into Bijia Peak about 3 nmi short of the runway at an altitude of 660 ft, below the 1,440 ft minimum safe altitude.

title: Garuda Indonesia 152
summary: Airbus A300 crashed into mountainous woodlands during approach to Medan after the crew became confused about the correct approach direction. Air traffic control issued conflicting instructions and called the aircraft by the wrong callsign, causing the crew to disregard a critical instruction about approach direction. The crew, unfamiliar with the analog flight instrumentation on the A300B4 FFCC, lost vertical awareness while concentrating on lateral changes and descended below the assigned 2000 foot altitude, striking treetops at 1550 feet.
probable_cause: Confusion regarding approach direction resulted in the crew initiating a left turn instead of a right turn during radar vectoring. This confusion, combined with the crew's focus on lateral changes and inadequate vertical monitoring, caused descent below assigned altitude. Contributing factors included poor ATC vectoring, inadequate conversion training for pilots switching between A300 models with different instrumentation, and failure of the GPWS system.

factors.evidence: ATC initially issued instruction using wrong callsign causing crew to disregard instruction about approach direction from south side of runway.
Crew believed they were flying approach on north side of airport per approach chart, but ATC intended south side approach.
Crew's vertical awareness reduced while concentrating on aircraft's lateral changes during confused approach.
First officer distracted during turn and did not notice aircraft turning left when right turn was expected.
GPWS system failed for undetermined reasons and did not provide ground proximity warning.
Aircraft struck treetops at 1550 feet above mean sea level in mountainous woodlands.

events.text: Medan ATC clears Flight 152 for ILS approach to runway 5 from 316 degree heading, instructs crew to turn left to 240 degrees to intercept ILS localizer.
ATC instructs crew to turn further left to 215 degrees for continued vectoring.
Medan ATC instructs crew to descend to 2000 feet and turn right heading 046 degrees to line up for runway 05, but controller confused about aircraft identity with another Flight 152 in area.
ATC initially uses wrong callsign Merpati 152, crew disregards instruction, ATC then queries with correct callsign Indonesia 152 but fails to repeat that approach would be on south side of runway.
Crew believes they are flying approach on north side of airport per approach chart, captain initiates left turn to 046 heading instead of right turn as instructed.
First officer distracted during turn, does not notice aircraft turning left for a while when right turn was expected.
Aircraft descends below assigned 2000 foot altitude while crew concentrating on lateral changes and losing vertical awareness.
Aircraft strikes treetops at 1550 feet above mean sea level in mountainous woodlands near Buah Nabar, GPWS system fails and provides no warning.

title: Aerosvit 241
summary: The aircraft entered Greek airspace and the crew mistook an ATC message intended for another aircraft. During the approach to Thessaloniki, the crew became disoriented and lost, failing to follow the proper approach route. Despite numerous cues from ATC and multiple opportunities to declare an emergency, the confused crew refused to declare emergency and attempted to re-orient themselves. The aircraft crashed into a mountainside during the second approach.
probable_cause: The flight crew's navigational error caused the crew to become disoriented and lost during the second approach to Thessaloniki. The crew failed to follow the route that they were supposed to take and did not declare emergency despite being in a difficult situation.

factors.evidence: The crew immediately contacted Thessaloniki Approach and mistook a message for an Olympic Airways flight, thinking the descent instruction was for them
The aircraft somehow arrived in Thessaloniki at a very high altitude and continued to pass over the airport, heading south; the controller noticed this and informed the crew

During the second approach, the controller repeatedly asked about their position for confirmation; the crew didn't report any problems regarding the approach procedure but suddenly requested a radar vector
The crew stated they were on the right track when based on ATC information they should have been north of the airport
The crew failed to follow the route that they were supposed to take and the aircraft ultimately crashed onto the mountains
Despite numerous cues, the confused crew refused to declare emergency over the situation
The aircraft was designed with Eastern European navigation system different from Western systems; there was no evidence that required modifications had been conducted for VOR-DME-ILS approach
The aircraft flew into a mountainside during the missed approach

events.text: Flight 241 entered Greek airspace and immediately contacted Thessaloniki Approach; the crew mistook a descent message intended for an Olympic Airways flight
The aircraft arrived at a very high altitude and continued to pass over the airport, heading south; the controller noticed and informed the crew they were off course
The crew was instructed to climb to 6000 feet and maintain position in the south holding pattern, then instructed to turn back to the airport's VOR
During the second approach, the controller repeatedly asked about their position; the crew stated they were on the right track and should have been north of the airport
The crew suddenly requested a radar vector to the controller; since Thessaloniki had no radar, the controller refused and asked the crew to comply with the written procedure
The aircraft flew into a mountainside during the second approach while attempting to re-orient themselves

title: SilkAir 185
summary: SilkAir Flight 185 departed Jakarta at 15:37 local time for an 80-minute flight to Singapore. At 16:05, the cockpit voice recorder ceased recording after Captain Tsu stated he was leaving the cockpit to fetch water. The flight data recorder also stopped recording at 16:11. Flight 185 remained level at FL350 until it started a rapid and nearly vertical dive around 16:12. Parts of the aircraft separated from the fuselage due to high forces from the nearly supersonic dive, and the aircraft hit the Musi River, killing all 104 people on board.
probable_cause: The NTSC concluded that the evidence was insufficient to determine a cause. The NTSB concluded that the crash was the result of deliberate flight-control inputs, most likely by the captain. Investigators found that flight inputs had moved the horizontal stabilizer from level flight to a full nose-down descent.

factors.evidence: Investigators found that flight inputs from one of the pilots had moved the stabilizer from level flight to a full nose-down descent.
It is likely that Captain Tsu pulled out the CVR circuit breaker while exiting the cockpit.
The FDR stopped recording at 16:11, and if Captain Tsu was responsible for the crash, he must have devised some excuse to persuade the first officer to leave the flight deck.
The aircraft started a rapid and nearly vertical dive, and parts of the aircraft separated from the fuselage due to high forces from the nearly supersonic dive.

events.text: The Boeing 737 departed Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport's runway 25R for an 80-minute flight to Singapore's Changi Airport.
The cockpit voice recorder ceased recording after Captain Tsu stated he was leaving the cockpit to fetch water.
The flight data recorder stopped recording.
The aircraft started a rapid and nearly vertical dive around 16:12.
The aircraft hit the Musi River near Palembang, Sumatra, and was travelling faster than the speed of sound.

title: China Airlines 676
summary: An Airbus A300 on ILS/DME approach to Taipei was 1000 ft above the normal glide slope. During go-around, the autopilot disengaged but the captain was unaware. The aircraft climbed steeply and stalled at 2751 ft. All 196 people on board were killed when it crashed into a residential area.
probable_cause: Pilot error: the captain was unaware the autopilot had disengaged during go-around and made no input to control the aircraft, which subsequently stalled.

factors.evidence: Aircraft was more than 300 m above its normal altitude and crew continued the approach.
The autopilot was disengaged but the pilot was not aware of it, leaving aircraft under no one's control for 11 seconds.
Pilot did not actively take control during go-around because he thought the autopilot would initiate the maneuver.
Aircraft reached 42.7 degree pitch-up angle with 45 knot speed and stalled at 2751 ft.
Aircraft fell and crashed into ground 200 ft left of runway, hitting houses and exploding.

events.text: Aircraft was 1000 ft too high above glide slope at 1.2 nautical miles short of runway in light rain and fog.
Go-around power applied, landing gear raised, flaps set to 20 degrees as aircraft climbed at 35 degree pitch-up angle.
Aircraft reached 42.7 degree pitch-up angle at 2751 ft with 45 knot speed and stalled.
Aircraft crashed into residential area 200 ft left of runway, hitting houses and exploding with all 196 killed.

notes: autopilot disengaged and pilot unaware
go-around at low altitude led to stall

title: Cubana de Aviación 389
summary: The Tu-154M overran the runway during takeoff from Quito after the nose failed to rotate at VR speed. The aircraft experienced two failed takeoff attempts before a third attempt was made. During the final attempt the nose would not lift despite reaching VR speed, forcing a rejected takeoff that the aircraft could not stop in time. The aircraft overran and crashed into buildings and a soccer field where post-crash fire killed many survivors.
probable_cause: When the aircraft reached VR speed on the third takeoff attempt, the nose of the aircraft would not rotate. The crew rejected the takeoff but the aircraft overran the runway end.

factors.evidence: When Flight 389 reached VR speed, the nose of the aircraft wouldn't rotate (lift)
During the first engine start a pneumatic valve was blocked; two engines were started with ground power and third engine started during taxi
The aircraft overran the runway, narrowly missed the heavily traveled Tufiño avenue, slammed into a wall, clipped an auto mechanic shop, smashed into two houses and plowed into a soccer field
The aircraft exploded and burst into flames; the post-crash fire was more determinant in the tragedy than the actual runway overrun

events.text: During first engine start a pneumatic valve was blocked; the problem was rectified and two engines started with ground power
Third engine was started during taxi as aircraft prepared for takeoff
Flight 389 obtained takeoff clearance and started first takeoff roll which then failed
Second takeoff attempt commenced and then failed before VR speed reached
Third takeoff attempt made and aircraft reached VR speed but nose of aircraft wouldn't rotate (lift)
Crew initiated rejected takeoff procedure but aircraft overran the runway at the end
Aircraft slammed into wall, mechanic shop, two houses and plowed into soccer field; aircraft exploded and burst into flames

notes: Root cause of takeoff failure not stated in text

title: Swissair 111
summary: Swissair Flight 111, an MD-11 flying from New York to Geneva, crashed into the Atlantic Ocean off Peggys Cove, Nova Scotia, on 2 September 1998 after smoke was detected in the cockpit and the crew diverted toward Halifax, killing all 229 aboard. Canada's TSB found that flammable material in the aircraft's structure let the fire spread beyond the crew's control; following the smoke checklist, the crew shut off the cabin bus and recirculation fans, which let the fire reach the cockpit and disable the flight instruments and autopilot before the aircraft struck the water.
probable_cause: The TSB concluded that flammable material used in the aircraft's structure allowed an in-flight fire to spread beyond the flight crew's control, disabling flight instruments and the autopilot and leading to loss of control before impact with the ocean.

factors.evidence: Flammable material used in the aircraft's structure allowed a fire to spread beyond the control of the flight crew, resulting in the crash of the aircraft.
The flight crew detected an odour in the cockpit and determined it to be smoke from the air conditioning system, and smoke became visible four minutes later.

In accordance with the Swissair checklist 'Smoke/fumes of unknown origin', the flight crew shut off power to the cabin using the 'CABIN BUS' switch, which also turned off the recirculating fans, allowing the fire to spread to the cockpit.
In a smoke-filled cockpit and with almost no flight instruments and little to no view outside, Löw may have become spatially disoriented.
Flight 111 struck the ocean at an estimated speed of 345 mph near St. Margarets Bay, killing all 215 passengers and 14 crew members on board.

events.text: At 22:10 ADT while flying over Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, the flight crew detected an odour in the cockpit and determined it was smoke from the air conditioning system.
Four minutes later the odour returned and smoke became visible, prompting the pilots to make a pan-pan call to Moncton Centre and request a diversion.

Following the Swissair 'Smoke/fumes of unknown origin' checklist, the crew shut off power to the cabin using the CABIN BUS switch, which also turned off the recirculating fans and allowed the fire to spread toward the cockpit.
At 22:24:28 the crew reported 'we now must fly manually' as the fire cut power to the autopilot, then declared an emergency ten seconds later in the last transmission received from Flight 111.

In a smoke-filled cockpit with almost no flight instruments, First Officer Löw may have become spatially disoriented, and the aircraft struck the ocean near St. Margarets Bay at an estimated 345 mph at 22:31:18 ADT.

title: Thai Airways International 261
summary: Domestic flight stalled and crashed into a swamp during third landing attempt after multiple go-arounds. Crew became upset after repeated failed approaches, causing disorientation. During go-around the angle of attack gradually increased to 48 degrees, leading to aerodynamic stall and loss of control into the swamp.
probable_cause: Crew disorientation and loss of situational awareness after multiple failed landing attempts, resulting in inadequate monitoring of aircraft attitude.

factors.evidence: the pilots attempted to land the aircraft but then decided to go-around for a second approach
the visibility decreased from 1,500 to 1,000 m which was now less than allowed for the type of non-precision approach in use
the crew became upset, causing them not to maintain awareness of the condition of their aircraft
During the go-around, the angle of attack of the aircraft gradually increased from 18 degrees to 48 degrees
the pilots failed to recover the aircraft and the aircraft crashed into the swamp

events.text: At 18:42 local time, the runway was sighted and the pilots attempted to land the aircraft
They then decided to go-around for a second approach
At 19:05 local time, the flight crews were informed of the weather in the area, which had deteriorated, with visibility decreased from 1,500 to 1,000 m
During the go-around, the angle of attack of the aircraft gradually increased from 18 degrees to 48 degrees
The pilots failed to recover the aircraft and the aircraft crashed into the swamp

title: China Southwest Airlines 4509
summary: Flight 4509, a Tupolev Tu-154M flying Chengdu-Wenzhou, was on approach when the crew extended flaps at 1,000 m; seconds later the nose dropped abruptly and the aircraft disintegrated in mid-air before crashing into high ground near Rui'an and exploding, killing all 61 aboard. The investigation found incorrect self-locking locknuts had been installed in the elevator system without maintenance crews noticing; the nuts worked loose in flight, leaving the elevator uncontrollable and disabling the pitch channel.
probable_cause: Incorrect self-locking locknuts installed in the elevator operating system went unnoticed by maintenance crews and spun off during the flight, leaving the elevator uncontrollable and disabling the pitch channel, causing the crash.

factors.evidence: Incorrect self-locking locknuts had been installed in the elevator operating system, which maintenance crews failed to notice
This disabled the aircraft's pitch channel, causing the crash
the aircraft's nose lowered abruptly, the aircraft disintegrated in mid-air and crashed into an area of high ground, and exploded

events.text: On 24 February 1999 the crew was preparing the aircraft for landing at Wenzhou Airport, and the flaps were extended at 1,000 m.
Seconds after flap extension, the aircraft's nose lowered abruptly, and it disintegrated in mid-air before crashing into high ground and exploding.
Investigators found incorrect self-locking locknuts in the elevator operating system, unnoticed by maintenance crews, had spun off during the flight, disabling the pitch channel.

title: LAPA 3142

title: 2012 Mount Salak Sukhoi Superjet crash
summary: On 9 May 2012, a Sukhoi Superjet 100 on a demonstration flight from Jakarta's Halim Airport crashed into Mount Salak, killing all 45 aboard. While orbiting near the 7,254 ft mountain during a descent from 10,000 to 6,000 ft, the EGPWS sounded 'Terrain Ahead, Pull Up' and repeated 'Avoid Terrain' alerts, but the crew, distracted by conversation with prospective airline customers on the flight deck and unable to see the terrain through thick cloud cover, disabled the warning believing it was a database fault; the aircraft struck the mountain moments later.

events.text: The SSJ-100 departed Halim Perdanakusuma Airport at 14:00 local time on its second demonstration flight of the day, carrying six crew, two Sukhoi representatives and 37 passengers.
At 14:26 the crew requested and were granted descent from 10,000 ft to 6,000 ft.
Two minutes later the crew requested and were approved to 'orbit to the right,' the last contact ATC had with the aircraft, then near 7,254 ft Mount Salak, higher than the requested flight level.
Four minutes into the orbit, the EGPWS sounded a 'Terrain Ahead, Pull Up' alert, followed immediately by a repeating 'Avoid Terrain' warning.
The pilots briefly discussed the warning and disabled it, believing it was a problem with the system's terrain database.
Less than 30 seconds later, a 'Gear Not Down' aural alert sounded, signifying the aircraft was too close to the ground without its landing gear lowered.
The captain disengaged the autopilot and put the aircraft into a slight nose-up attitude not consistent with an evasive maneuver.
The captain told the first officer the autopilot was off, and impact with terrain occurred two seconds later at 14:33 local time.

title: Dana Air 992
summary: Dana Air Flight 992, a McDonnell Douglas MD-83 flying from Abuja to Lagos, suffered a dual-engine failure on approach to Murtala Muhammed International Airport on 3 June 2012 after incorrect assembly had severed the engines' fuel line, cutting off fuel delivery to both engines. The pilots did not declare an emergency until the second engine lost power on final approach, and lost situational awareness as the aircraft descended and crashed into buildings in the Iju-Ishaga neighbourhood, killing all 153 aboard and six people on the ground.

title: Malaysia Airlines 17 shootdown
summary: Malaysia Airlines Flight 17, a Boeing 777-200ER flying from Amsterdam to Kuala Lumpur, was shot down by a Buk 9M38 surface-to-air missile on 17 July 2014 while flying over territory in eastern Ukraine controlled by Russian-backed separatist forces during the war in Donbas. Contact was lost about 50 km from the Russia-Ukraine border, and wreckage fell near Hrabove in Donetsk Oblast. title: Germanwings 9525
summary: Germanwings Flight 9525, an Airbus A320-211 with 150 people aboard, was deliberately crashed by first officer Andreas Lubitz into a mountain in the French Alps on 24 March 2015. After the captain left the cockpit for a scheduled break, Lubitz locked the cockpit door and set the aircraft to descend. summary: Metrojet Flight 9268, an Airbus A321 charter flying tourists from Sharm El Sheikh to Saint Petersburg, exploded above the northern Sinai Peninsula on 31 October 2015 and crashed, killing all 224 people aboard. Flightradar24 data showed the aircraft climbing to 33,500 ft at 404 knots before suddenly descending to 28,375 ft at 62 knots about 50 km northeast of Nekhel, after which its position was no longer tracked.

Wreckage was scattered over 20 square kilometers, with the forward section about 5 km from the tail, indicating the aircraft had disintegrated in flight; aerial images showed the wings remained intact until impact.

The Islamic State's Sinai branch claimed responsibility for the crash, and Russian investigators concluded the most likely cause was an onboard explosive device that killed all 224 passengers and crew.
